Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

1. I believe that the recording sites between hemispheres must be matched; this is the only way to ensure that the inter-hemispheric differences reported are not simply due to the intra-hemispheric differences reported in Supplementary Figures 1-2.

2. I'm a bit confused as to why the landmark used in Supplementary Figures 1-2 is the dorsal aspect of the central sulcus. I might expect that premotor electrodes would generalize better (and exhibit more bilateral encoding) than M1 electrodes, but your analysis seems to make the argument that face M1 electrodes also generalize better than arm M1 electrodes. Could you provide a bit more interpretation of this empirical result?

3. I don't quite get the relevance of Churchland 2012 results to the trace in Figure 5C. Churchland et al. used only outward reaches in the 2012 study, whereas your subjects are performing out-and-back movements. The trace in Figure 5C is more similar to the trigger signal reported in Kaufman, et al. In fact, in monkeys making movement sequences (comparable to your out-and-back movements), Zimnik and Churchland (2021) found a biphasic trigger signal that looks pretty similar to the trace shown in 5C. To that end, it might be useful to plot the across-subject hand speeds in 5C. If the ECoG signal plotted is related to the trigger signal, then it should have a time-course similar to the subjects' hand speed.

4. Related to 5C, wouldn't it make more sense to plot the actual HFA amplitude, rather than the predicted HFA amplitude? I understand that the two will likely be very similar, but 5C is making a point about the true neural activity.

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Left Hemisphere Dominance for Bilateral Kinematic Encoding in the Human Brain" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been evaluated by Tirin Moore as the Senior Editor, a Reviewing Editor, and the original reviewers.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed, as outlined below:

1. All reviewers were very happy with the revisions and think the paper is strong. Please see the remaining comments of Reviewer #2 especially with respect to statistical support for some of the claims.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors have made a profound and detailed attempt to comply with the questions raised by the reviewers. Accordingly, as far as I am concerned, the paper is acceptable for publication in eLife.

This is important work in which data is obtained from a unique set of patients to reveal the control of ipsilateral and contralateral arm movement in a very detailed manner. It complements previous work collected from nonhuman primates.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors adequately addressed most of my previous concerns. I have one further recommendation and a comment related to the modification.

The authors need some statistical support for their claims regarding (i) hemispheric equality in regional distribution of electrodes (lines 226-228) and (ii) hemispheric difference in the number of electrodes with good/poor across-arm generalization (lines 412-414, 439-441, and 590-597).

(i) Hemispheric equality in regional distribution of electrodes (lines 226-228):

"When the categorization data were pooled across the three left hemisphere and three right hemisphere patients, the proportion of electrodes was similar in premotor, sensorimotor motor, and parietal regions." (Lines 226-228)

This can be tested by using, for example, multinomial goodness-of-fit tests using expected frequency for each region estimated from the data from either hemisphere. Reporting the number or proportion (%) for these three regions in the main text, in addition to the bar graphs, would also be helpful.

(ii) Hemispheric difference in number of electrodes with good/poor across-arm generalization (lines 412-414, 439-441, and 590-597):

"This categorization scheme revealed a striking anatomical division, with electrodes showing good across-arm generalization clustering in the left premotor and superior parietal regions and electrodes that generalized poorly clustering in left and right M1. This result does not appear to reflect a sampling bias. There are more left hemisphere electrodes compared to right hemisphere electrodes because two of the left hemisphere patients had high density grid implants. However, the electrodes in our left and right hemisphere samples were similarly distributed over premotor, sensorimotor and parietal regions (see Supplementary Figure 2)." (Lines 590-597)

The fact that the electrodes in the left and right hemispheres have similar distribution over these regions does not automatically protect from the risk of finding more electrodes in the left hemisphere due to the hemispheric bias in electrode number, and need formal statistical tests. Similarly to the first point above, this can be tested by using goodness-of-fit tests (e.g., chi-squared test, likelihood-ratio G test, etc.) using the expected number of electrodes that should be found in the same region in the other hemisphere under the null-hypothesis of hemispheric symmetry (e.g., if 20 electrodes are found in the left hemisphere, 74*20/141 electrodes should also be found in the right).

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

Merrick et al. were admirably responsive to all reviewer comments, and the manuscript has been greatly improved as a result. I have no further critiques.

results.result: Participants successfully performed the reaching task with low error rates (0-12.5% unsuccessful trials), bell-shaped velocity profiles, and comparable spatial accuracy between left and right arms (mean distance from target center: 0.80 cm for right arm, 0.90 cm for left arm, p=0.22).
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C23 provide converging behavioral evidence that participants performed the task successfully and comparably with both arms. The statistical test (C23) confirms no significant difference in accuracy between arms, supporting the validity of the experimental paradigm.

results.result: A substantial proportion of electrodes showed predictive encoding of arm movements (31% for contralateral, 25% for ipsilateral, 24% for both), with similar electrode distributions across premotor, sensorimotor, and parietal regions in both hemispheres.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 establish that the encoding model successfully predicts neural activity for both contralateral and ipsilateral movements across multiple brain regions. The chi-square test (C27, p=0.99) confirms comparable electrode coverage between hemispheres, addressing potential sampling bias concerns.

results.result: The left hemisphere shows stronger bilateral encoding than the right hemisphere, with lower contralateral bias scores (p<0.001) and this bias weakening with distance from primary motor cortex in both hemispheres.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 demonstrate a key hemispheric asymmetry through multiple statistical tests. The significant Arm×Hemisphere interaction (C30) and permutation test results (C31) provide strong evidence for left hemisphere dominance in bilateral encoding. The spatial gradient analysis (C32) adds anatomical specificity to this finding.

results.result: Hemispheric asymmetries in bilateral encoding vary by task phase: the left hemisphere shows stronger bilateral encoding during movement execution (contralateral bias disappears, p=0.482), while the right hemisphere shows stronger bilateral encoding during instruction.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C39 reveal a complex three-way interaction (C35, p<0.001) between Arm, Hemisphere, and Task Phase. The statistical tests consistently support opposing temporal patterns between hemispheres, with the left hemisphere showing remarkable bilateral symmetry during movement (C37, C38).

results.result: Across-arm generalization is better in the left hemisphere than the right (R²left=0.04 vs R²right=0.11, p<0.001), with better generalization during instruction than movement phase in both hemispheres.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C47 demonstrate superior across-arm generalization in the left hemisphere through multiple statistical comparisons. The three-way interaction (C43) and simple effects analyses (C46, C47) provide robust evidence for both hemispheric and temporal differences in representational overlap.

results.result: Electrodes showing good across-arm generalization are predominantly located in left hemisphere premotor and parietal cortices, while electrodes showing poor generalization cluster bilaterally near the central sulcus (M1), with generalization quality correlating with distance from dorsal central sulcus in the left hemisphere (r=0.46, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C55 establish a clear anatomical dissociation between electrode types. The chi-square test (C50, p<0.001) confirms left hemisphere predominance for good generalizers, while spatial correlation analyses (C54, C55) link generalization quality to anatomical location. The 61% of poor generalizers meeting encoding criteria (C49) rules out the alternative explanation that poor generalization simply reflects weak ipsilateral encoding.

results.result: Electrodes that generalize well across arms show greater tuning similarity (p<0.001), with this similarity being higher during movement for good generalizers but higher during instruction for poor generalizers, while both electrode types show main effects of arm and task phase on modulation depth.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60 demonstrate that representational overlap differs qualitatively between electrode types. The significant interaction and simple effects analyses (C58-C60) reveal opposing temporal dynamics of tuning similarity, suggesting fundamentally different computational roles for these electrode populations.

results.result: Speed and position features dominate the encoding model (68% contralateral, 63% ipsilateral contribution), with electrodes that generalize well showing strongest correspondence to position (200ms lag for contralateral, 150ms for ipsilateral) while poor generalizers correspond most to speed (200ms lag for both arms).
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C69 characterize the kinematic features driving neural predictions. The relative contributions (C62, C63) and cross-correlation analyses (C65-C69) are clearly stated with specific lag times. The comparison to primate studies (C64) provides external validation, though this relies on citation rather than direct data.

results.result: The left hemisphere shows substantially stronger ipsilateral encoding (Cohen's d=1.34) and greater representational overlap between arms, with good generalizers clustering in left premotor/parietal regions and poor generalizers in bilateral M1, where divergence occurs during instruction via ipsilateral inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C75 synthesize the main findings with a large effect size (C72) supporting the hemispheric asymmetry. The anatomical clustering patterns (C73, C74) and temporal dynamics (C75) are consistently supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: Target tuning exists for both contralateral and ipsilateral movements, with ipsilateral tuning being shallower overall, but electrodes that generalize well show similar spatial tuning for both arms while poor generalizers (primarily in M1) show disparate tuning.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 and C84 establish differential tuning properties between electrode types. While the statistical tests supporting 'significantly shallower' (C79) are not explicitly provided, the qualitative pattern is clearly described and the inference about directional encoding (C81) follows logically from the similar tuning observation (C80).

results.result: The encoding model successfully predicts neural activity during the instruction phase, confirming movement planning, with the left hemisphere showing stronger bilateral encoding overall but with opposing temporal patterns between hemispheres (left: stronger during movement; right: stronger during instruction), and complete disappearance of contralateral bias in the left hemisphere during movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88 integrate findings about task phase effects. The ability to predict activity during instruction (C85) validates the delayed-response paradigm. The hemispheric differences (C86-C88) are supported by the statistical analyses presented earlier, though C88's claim of 'complete disappearance' is strong given the p=0.482 result.

results.result: The observed left hemisphere asymmetry in bilateral encoding aligns with established literature on left hemisphere dominance in praxis, apraxia following left hemisphere lesions affecting both limbs, and functional imaging showing left hemisphere activation during ipsilateral movement, with ipsilateral encoding most prominent in left premotor and parietal cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C98 contextualize the findings within the apraxia and praxis literature. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations (C90-C97) and the anatomical overlap with praxis regions (C98) is directly demonstrated in the data. However, the authors acknowledge (in discussion) that their simple reaching task differs from typical praxis tasks.

results.result: Using a kinematic encoding model, the study demonstrates that the left hemisphere more strongly encodes the ipsilateral arm than the right hemisphere during both preparation and movement, with this asymmetry driven by electrodes over premotor and parietal cortices while sensorimotor cortex shows strong contralateral encoding.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107 summarize the main conclusion. These are well-supported by the extensive statistical analyses presented throughout the results section (C28-C47, C70-C74). The anatomical specificity (C106, C107) is demonstrated through the spatial analyses and electrode categorization.

results.result: The study recorded from six epilepsy patients (three per hemisphere) across three hospitals, with 665 electrodes remaining after quality control (82 removed for noise, 5 for epileptic activity), and kinematic reconstruction showed high correlation with Leap motion data (r=0.98 for position, r=0.93 for velocity).
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 describe the dataset and methods. The sample characteristics are clearly stated (C108, C109), quality control procedures are documented (C110), and kinematic validation is quantified (C111). These provide essential methodological transparency, though the small sample size (n=6, 3 per hemisphere) limits generalizability.

results.result: Alternative explanations for ipsilateral encoding include postural control (though evidence suggests right hemisphere specialization and timing mismatch) and bimanual coordination (with left hemisphere showing greater impairments post-stroke and fMRI evidence for maintained ipsilateral representations in premotor/parietal regions during bimanual tasks).
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C104 discuss alternative interpretations based on cited literature. While the citations support these possibilities, the current study lacks the experimental manipulations (EMG, postural measurements, bimanual conditions) needed to directly test these alternatives. The authors acknowledge these limitations but cannot definitively rule out these explanations.

results.result: The introduction establishes that while motor control is primarily contralateral, ipsilateral hemisphere activity contains movement-relevant information that can be decoded, with evidence for both overlap and independence hypotheses depending on task and region, and known hemispheric asymmetries in praxis favoring the left hemisphere.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C17 provide background context through citations. These establish the scientific foundation for the study by reviewing prior work on contralateral organization (C1-C2), bilateral activity (C3-C6), representational overlap/independence (C7-C11), and hemispheric asymmetries (C12-C15).
